module_title: Introduction to Financial Markets and Its Two Pillars
introduction: A Financial Market is a platform or system where funds are exchanged between 'Savers' (Investors/Households) and 'Borrowers' (Businesses/Government). Based on the 'Time Period' of the funds being borrowed/lent, the market is broadly divided into two categories: the Money Market and the Capital Market.

core_concepts.title: Money Market
core_concepts.description: This is the market for 'Short-term' borrowing and lending. The maximum maturity period for transactions here is '1 year or less' (up to 364 days). It is primarily used to fulfill the daily working capital requirements of banks, corporates, and the government.

core_concepts.title: Capital Market
core_concepts.description: This is the market for raising 'Long-term' funds. The maturity period for transactions here is 'more than 1 year' (e.g., 5 years, 10 years, or perpetual). It is used for long-term investments like setting up factories, buying machinery, or business expansion.

core_concepts.title: The Regulators
core_concepts.description:
1. The Money Market is regulated by the 'Reserve Bank of India (RBI)'. 
2. The Capital Market is regulated by the 'Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)'.

core_concepts.title: Risk and Liquidity
core_concepts.description: Since the duration is short, Money Market instruments carry 'Low Risk' and 'High Liquidity' (can be converted to cash instantly). Capital Market instruments have a longer duration, hence they carry 'Higher Risk' and relatively 'Lower Liquidity'.

important_entities.name: Liquidity
important_entities.significance: In financial markets, liquidity refers to how quickly you can convert an investment back into hard cash without suffering a massive loss in value. The Money Market is highly liquid.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A very common exam trap: 'The Stock Market is regulated by the RBI.' This is FALSE. The Stock Market is a part of the Capital Market, and therefore, it is strictly regulated by SEBI, not the RBI.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Pocket Money = Short Term, Business Capital = Long Term
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Money (like pocket money) gets spent quickly (up to 1 year). Capital is invested for the long haul (> 1 year).

exam_strategy_tips: In NISM and Banking exams, direct questions are asked on maturity periods. Remember: An instrument with a 364-day maturity belongs to the 'Money Market', but a 366-day instrument belongs to the 'Capital Market'.
